They gave every dot a seat number and a walking speed. ð§® ð

This is agent-based simulation, the same modeling airport planners run before a terminal exists. Each digital passenger carries its own pace, its own bag, its own hesitation at the overhead bin, and the software plays the whole boarding out inside the drawing.

The reason is money. Boarding sits on the critical path of an aircraft turnaround, and industry research prices a jet parked at a terminal at roughly $30 a minute. Planning figures give deplaning 20 passengers a minute through one door. Boarding manages 12.

So the gate, the bridge and the holdroom get tested against IATA Level of Service standards while all three are still lines on a screen.

One layout. Thousands of simulated boardings. Zero concrete poured.

Cyber Exploring Iran - a walk through open and publicly available systems

Needed a brain break from writing and figured I'd look through the open cameras and systems in Iran using Shodan 

So many more systems online now compared to just a couple weeks ago. Looks like, for the most part, they are fully back online after the Internet being shutdown for a long time

Cyber Exploring is kinda fun, using a computer search engine, like Shodan, that acts like Google but searches for computers and devices online instead of a normal search

Google is nice, because you can do an image search where it shows you open camera stills, and screen grabs of VNC and remote desktop systems

This just shows why it is so very important to turn public access OFF for any device you put online, and make sure to change the default password and update the device firmware

Because, like Roz from Monsters Inc says, someone is "ALWAYS watching"

*** Disclaimer: All pictures are from Shodan's screenshot service. No systems were accessed for this post. Never access a system that you do not have permission to access

Ukraineâs Ministry of Defense launched TrophyLab on June 19, 2026 â a government platform that gives verified researchers, defense companies, and allied governments access to captured Russian weapons. The catalog covers more than 115 trophy samples across dozens of categories, including drones, missiles, tanks, armored vehicles, and electronic warfare systems, complete with blueprints, technical data, and analysis results.

What makes TrophyLab unusual is that partners can also request the actual physical hardware for testing. Formats range from non-destructive examination all the way to full disassembly or destruction of the component, letting engineers build and test countermeasures against real enemy equipment. The platform pools intelligence from Ukraineâs Defense Forces, its Main Intelligence Directorate, and the Security Service of Ukraine.

Most countries keep captured enemy tech secret to hold a military edge â Ukraine is doing the opposite. Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov framed it as turning battlefield seizures into shared knowledge, saying âevery missile, drone, and vehicle seized on the battlefield is now a source of knowledge for the free world.â The goal is to shorten the time it takes allies to develop defenses against Russian weapons systems.

China may have just removed one of the biggest manufacturing barriers around a fascinating form of graphene. âï¸

Rhombohedral graphene is ordinary carbon arranged in an unusual staircase-like stacking pattern. That tiny structural difference can produce remarkable electronic behavior, including strongly correlated and superconducting states that researchers are exploring for future quantum technologies.

The problem? This stacking arrangement has historically been extremely difficult to produce reliably.

Researchers at Peking University developed a way to grow rhombohedral multilayer graphene using a specially engineered copperânickel alloy surface. Instead of searching through rare flakes and hoping to find the right stacking order, the substrate helps guide the graphene into the desired structure during growth.

The reported result: more than 99% rhombohedral stacking purity.

That matters because reproducible, high-quality material is essential before scientists can seriously explore scalable devices based on its unusual quantum properties.

But thereâs an important distinction: this does not mean China has already mass-produced graphene quantum computers or solved fault-tolerant quantum computing.

What researchers may have solved is a much earlierâand crucialâproblem:

How do you reliably manufacture the material needed to investigate these possibilities at scale?

Sometimes the biggest breakthrough isnât building the final computer.

Itâs finally learning how to make the material the computer might someday need. ð¬âï¸

When most students were planning their careers, Anagha Rajesh was asking a question that could redefine the future of computing:

What if the world's data could be stored inside DNA?

While pursuing Chemistry at BITS Goa, Anagha discovered that scientists had been exploring DNA data storage for decades. The idea fascinated her. Instead of pursuing a conventional PhD path, she decided to chase a moonshot.

In 2024, she founded BioCompute, a deep-tech startup building DNA-based data storage systems that could make future data centers far smaller and more energy-efficient.

Starting with grants, a small team, and even a home lab, BioCompute spent months experimenting at the intersection of biology and computing. In 2025, the startup achieved a major breakthroughâsuccessfully writing digital data into DNA and retrieving it back, proving that its core technology worked.

The startup soon attracted backing from investors including 1517 Fund, gradCapital, and Emergent Ventures, helping it build an end-to-end prototype for DNA data storage. Over two years, the team conducted thousands of experiments and established India's first dedicated lab pursuing DNA data storage at this scale.

Today, BioCompute is developing DNA storage chips that could transform how humanity stores information. As the company enters its next phase, Anagha has relocated operations to San Francisco to access the capital, talent, and deep-tech ecosystem needed to compete globally.

The launch of the DeepSeek-V4-Flash API in public beta is causing serious concern among major tech labs. The new model delivers frontier-level performance at costs so low they almost seem like a typo.

Here is a breakdown of what makes this drop a game-changer:

Massive Cost Disruption
DeepSeek-V4-Flash comes in at just $0.14 per 1M input tokens and $0.28 per 1M output tokens. For comparison, competing top-tier models charge up to $10 input and $50 output, making Flash roughly 36x cheaper on input and 89x cheaper on output while holding its own on benchmark accuracy.

True Cost Efficiency
Even when measuring total cost per completed task rather than token pricingâwhere additional agent steps can accumulateâdata shows DeepSeek completing identical benchmark tasks at 105x lower cost than models like Fable 5. Average task execution drops to roughly $0.03.

Upgraded Agent & Developer Capabilities
The official V4-Flash release brings massive leaps in agent capabilities over previous previews, natively supporting the Responses API format and full adaptation for Codex integration. On benchmark suites like Terminal Bench 2.1, it scores an 82.7, competing head-to-head with top-tier proprietary models.

The Somali piracy crisis hit its peak around 2009, when hijackings off the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean became so frequent that international shipping routes were forced to change entirely. Pirates were capturing everything from small fishing boats to massive oil tankers, often holding crews and cargo for ransom payments that sometimes reached millions of dollars per ship. What started as a response to illegal foreign fishing and dumping off Somaliaâs coast turned into a full scale criminal industry.

The scale of it forced a rare level of international cooperation, with naval forces from the US, EU, China, Russia and others all patrolling the same waters to try to contain it. Billions of dollars moved through ransom payments, insurance costs and military operations before hijackings finally started dropping off years later. It remains one of the clearest examples of how quickly lawlessness in international waters can spiral into a global economic problem.

Token streaming is why AI answers appear word by word instead of all at once.

The model writes one word at a time either way. Without streaming, every
finished word waits in a buffer until the last one is done, so you watch a
spinner for the full 3 seconds and read nothing.

With streaming, each word is flushed onto one held-open reply the moment it
exists. First word: 3.0s becomes 0.1s. Last word: 3.0s either way.

Streaming kills the wait, not the work.

Did you think streaming made the model faster? Save this for your next system
design interview, and send it to the dev on your team who is still buffering
the whole response.

Long before humans, space rocks slammed into Earth hard enough to leave marks we can still see today, some of them bigger than entire states. Take the one hiding under the ice and rock of Russia, punched out by an asteroid 36 million years ago, decades before scientists even connected the dots to the fossil record chaos it left behind. Or the crater in Ontario that's so old and so massive geologists spent years arguing over whether it was even from space at all, not volcanic activity. These impacts didn't just leave a hole, they reshaped climates, wiped out species, and in one case may have literally set the stage for mammals to take over the planet. The wildest part is how much time has erased: erosion, tectonic shifts, entire ice ages have worked to bury this evidence, yet scientists can still map out rings from impacts that happened over a billion years ago. Some of these craters are so wide you could stand at the center and not see the edge. And the biggest one on this list is so old it predates complex life on land entirely. It's strange to think the ground under certain unassuming towns and farmland is actually the scar tissue of a catastrophic collision that changed the course of evolution. Which one do you think left the deepest mark on life as we know it?

#asteroidimpact #earthscience #craters #deeptime #geology

Many of the world's largest container ships are 399.9 metres long instead of an even 400 metres for a surprisingly practical reason: infrastructure limits.

Ports, canals, dry docks, and maritime regulations often use 400 metres as an important design threshold. A ship officially measuring 400 metres or more may exceed the maximum size that certain berths, turning basins, locks, or dry docks were built to accommodate. By making a vessel just 10 centimetres shorter, shipbuilders ensure it falls within the "under 400 metres" category, allowing it to access more ports around the world without requiring expensive infrastructure upgrades or special exemptions.

Think of it like building a moving warehouse. Every extra metre allows more containers to be carried, making each voyage more profitable. But if adding just a few centimetres prevents the ship from entering major ports, the additional cargo is no longer worth the loss of flexibility.

This isn't unique to ships. Engineers frequently design structures and vehicles to sit just below important limits, whether it's aircraft wingspans, truck heights, or bridge clearances. The goal is to maximize capacity while remaining compatible with existing infrastructure.

So the famous 399.9-metre length isn't a coincidence or a marketing gimmick - it's an engineering compromise. It's just long enough to carry an enormous amount of cargo, yet just short enough to fit within the world's busiest ports and maritime facilities.

#knowledge #learning #explore #viral #relatable

REMIND is an appearance-based tracking system designed to recognize objects that disappear, reappear, look similar, or are viewed from different angles. The system also reports uncertainty when matches are ambiguous or provisional, making it useful for indoor robots, autonomous navigation, computer vision research, and long-term object tracking.

For decadesâ¦

â¦designing a custom chip meant access to expensive software, specialized engineers, and millions of dollars.

That barrier is getting lower.

Through the Google-sponsored Open MPW program, SkyWaterâs open-source SKY130 process, and tools like OpenROAD and OpenLane, individuals can design a real integrated circuit using free software and have it manufactured as part of a shared wafer run. Instead of paying for an entire silicon wafer, hundreds of projects share the manufacturing costs through a multi-project wafer (MPW) shuttle. 

The workflow is remarkably modern:

* Write hardware logic in Verilog.
* Run automated synthesis, placement, routing, and verification with open-source tools.
* Submit the design through a shuttle program.
* Receive a real fabricated chip months later.

The chips are manufactured using a 130 nm processâtechnology thatâs more than two decades old by todayâs standardsâbut itâs still ideal for education, research, embedded systems, sensors, and many custom digital designs. It isnât intended to compete with cutting-edge 3 nm AI GPUs, but it makes custom silicon accessible to students, researchers, and hobbyists. 

Why it matters:

* Free, open-source chip design tools are now practical for real silicon.
* Hundreds of independent projects can share one fabrication run.
* More than 600 tapeouts have already used the OpenROAD ecosystem.
* Developers can learn ASIC design without purchasing proprietary EDA software.
* Open hardware is becoming more accessible, much like open-source software did decades ago. 

The biggest breakthrough isnât that anyone can build the next NVIDIA GPU from a laptop.

Itâs that custom silicon is no longer reserved for large semiconductor companies. Open design tools, shared fabrication programs, and community-driven hardware projects are making chip development accessible to individuals in much the same way GitHub transformed software development.

He Exposes the Real Money Glitch

In Trust, J. Paul Getty calmly explains to his grandson how the family fortune actually works, and it sounds less like wealth and more like engineering.

The trust buys oil fields, the oil pays for tankers, the tankers fund refineries, the refineries feed gas stations, the gas stations support hotels, and every dollar those hotels generate flows straight back into the trust to buy more oil.

Nothing leaks.

Nothing idles.

And most importantly, nothing shows up as profit.

Getty makes the point brutally clear: Getty Oil never pays tax because, on paper, it never makes money, as every dollar is reinvested, absorbed, or cycled before it can be counted as profit for accounting purposes.

The grandson calls it a spiderâs web, and Getty agrees, because the system is designed so the money never escapes, only grows wider and stronger with each loop.

This scene lands hard because it reveals how extreme wealth is actually preserved, not by chasing income, but by controlling structure, flow, and ownership so tightly that taxation becomes almost irrelevant.

Most people focus on earning more and get punished for it.

The ultra-wealthy focus on design, keeping money in motion inside systems they own.

The real game isnât about how much you make.

Itâs about making sure the money never leaves.

In 2024, Akamai blocked 311 billion web attacks. Thatâs 850 million per day.

But the companyâs co-founder was stabbed to death on one of the 9/11 flights. While Danny Lewin was dying, his algorithm was being tested.

After the attacks, billions of people flooded news websites. Most crashed. The ones running Akamaiâs math stayed online.

Hereâs how it started:

In 1995, Tim Berners-Lee noticed a massive problem. When millions requested the same content, servers crashed. He called it the âWorld Wide Waitâ and challenged MIT colleagues to fix it.

Math professor Tom Leighton took up the challenge with his graduate student, Danny Lewin, a former Israeli special forces captain.

They built something called consistent hashing.

Imagine every piece of content and every server mapped to points on a massive ring. When you request a video, the system finds your request and serves it from the nearest server on the ring.

Traditional systems break when you add servers. Everything needs remapping.

Consistent hashing only remaps a fraction. Add 1,000 servers to a million-server network and only 0.1% of content moves.

That equation now powers 30% of global internet traffic.

Today Akamai runs 365,000 servers across 135 countries. 85% of internet users are within one network hop of their infrastructure. 

When you stream a video in New York from a London server, Akamai fetches it once, caches it locally, then serves millions from that copy. Data travels 50 miles instead of 3,000.

The numbers are staggering. 946 terabytes of attack data processed daily. 7 trillion DDoS attacks stopped. 

Every top streaming service. Every major bank. All six US military branches.

One algorithm, one target & the entire internet goes dark.

P.S.:In 2026, the biggest opportunities wonât come from thinking big. Theyâll come from solving something specific, better than anyone else.

At 21, Palmer Luckey sold Oculus to Facebook for $2 billion. 
Five years later, Facebook pushed him out.

Most people would've taken the money and gone quiet. He did the opposite he walked straight into the one industry Silicon Valley refused to touch: weapons.

While every other founder chased apps, ads and feeds, Luckey started Anduril to build autonomous drones and AI systems for the US military. 

The Valley thought defense was uninvestable and un-cool. He saw the opposite a massive market run by slow, decades-old contractors, with nobody from tech competing.

Then he rewrote the rules. Legacy defense giants only build after the government signs a contract. 
Anduril builds the weapon first, with its own money, 
then sells the finished product to the Pentagon. 

Faster, cheaper, and the risk sits on Anduril instead of the taxpayer.

That one inversion helped push the company to a ~$60 billion valuation in under a decade.
The lesson: the field everyone avoids usually has the least competition  if you're willing to be the one who walks in.

Balaji Srinivasan spent years arguing the future isn't nations  it's "network states." 

Communities that form online around shared values, then touch down in the real world with their own culture, economy, and eventually recognition.

Then he tried to build one. 

Network School a private csociety in Forest City, Malaysia, where founders, engineers and digital nomads from dozens of countries live, train and build together. Over RM100 million already invested, with a RM500 million expansion on the way.

This month, the experiment collided with something no whitepaper plans for: a sovereign government.
A viral social-media claim alleged some residents had entered Malaysia on second-country passports. 

The Home Ministry launched an immigration probe and inspected the campus. Within a day, immigration cleared all 266 foreign residents every document valid, no violations found, the allegation debunked.

But the fallout stuck. Balaji paused the entire Malaysian expansion, asked the Prime Minister's office for formal written assurances, and signaled he'd move the whole project to a friendlier country if it wasn't welcome.

That's the lesson under the drama. You can design a society online, but the moment it lands on real soil, it answers to real borders, real politics, and a state that was there first. The network state still runs on someone else's land.

Follow @founder.gyaan 
#NetworkState #Balaji

A Singapore-registered container ship, Nawata Bhum, collided with the embankment of the Hooghly River in West Bengal on Wednesday, August 12, while sailing towards Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port in Kolkata.

Videos circulating on social media show the container-laden vessel heading towards the riverbank without any visible reduction in speed or change in direction. The shipâs horn can be heard sounding repeatedly as it approaches the embankment. Moments later, its bow becomes lodged in the riverbank.

Footage reviewed by AsiaOne showed no other vessel immediately in the shipâs path when the incident occurred. The road alongside the embankment also appeared largely deserted, with no visible structural damage reported apart from affected vegetation.

According to vessel-tracking data from MarineTraffic, the ship made a right turn north of Latpatia at around 10:26 am (India time). Its declared next port of call was Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, formerly known as Kolkata Port.

For robots, autonomous driving, and drone mapping, open-source Glob3R turns large image collections into accurate and consistent 3D reconstructions.

Glob3R uses 3D foundation models to connect views across long sequences and complex scenes, then improves camera positions and scene geometry through motion averaging and bundle adjustment. It is designed to work with large-scale environments, unordered images, and challenging multi-view datasets.

This can help robots understand indoor and outdoor spaces, support autonomous vehicles with detailed environmental maps, and allow drones to reconstruct buildings, roads, construction sites, and large geographic areas in 3D.

A corroded lump of bronze sat in a shipwreck for two thousand years before anyone realized what it actually was. Sponge divers pulled it up in 1901 near a tiny Greek island, and for decades it just looked like scrap. Turns out it was a hand cranked computer. Inside a case roughly the size of a shoebox, ancient Greek engineers packed at least 30 tiny bronze gears, all working together to predict solar and lunar eclipses years before they happened. One dial even tracked the four year cycle of the ancient Olympic games, so this thing was part astronomer, part sports calendar. The wildest part is how it handled the moon. The moon doesnât move at a constant speed across the sky because its orbit is elliptical, and the mechanismâs makers accounted for that with a pin and slot gear system that speeds up and slows down just like the real thing. Nobody could even read the inscriptions on the corroded fragments until modern X-ray and CT scanners came along and let researchers peer inside the metal itself. And hereâs the part that still bugs historians, nothing this mechanically complex shows up again in the historical record for over a thousand years. Itâs like technology from the future got dropped into the ancient world and then vanished. The ship carrying it was loaded with bronze statues, glassware, and jewelry too, resting more than 150 feet down between Crete and the Greek mainland. So who built something this advanced, and why did it take a thousand years for anyone to catch up?

Steve Jobs once sent an email to himself that revealed a rarely seen side of the Apple co-founder.

At 11:08 p.m. on September 2, 2010, Jobs reflected on the countless people, discoveries and systems his life depended upon. From the food he ate and the language he spoke to the medicine and technology he used, he acknowledged that none of us succeeds entirely alone.

âI love and admire my species, living and dead, and am totally dependent on them for my life and well-being,â he wrote.

The message was sent roughly 13 months before Jobs died on October 5, 2011. Preserved by the Steve Jobs Archive, it offers a striking contrast to the popular idea of the self-made genius.

Behind one of historyâs most influential innovators was a man who understood a simple truth: every achievement is built upon the work of others.

Rich people donât always sell assets when they need cash.

Sometimes, they borrow against them.

Hereâs the basic idea:

Imagine you own a $1 million stock portfolio and want $200,000 for a home purchase.

Option one is to sell $200,000 worth of appreciated stock.

But selling can create a taxable capital gain, depending on your cost basis.

Option two is something wealthy investors often consider: borrowing against the portfolio through a securities-backed line of credit.

The stocks remain invested.

No stock sale means the borrowing itself generally doesnât create a capital-gains tax event.

And if the portfolio continues appreciating, the investor still participates in that upside.

But thereâs a part social media often leaves out.

This is not free money.

You pay interest.

The lender can change collateral requirements.

If your portfolio falls far enough, you may need to add collateral or repay part of the loan.

And borrowing against volatile assets can turn a market crash into a liquidity problem.

Thatâs the real lesson.

Wealthy people donât just think about what they own.

They think about how to access liquidity without unnecessarily disrupting the assets they want to keep compounding.

That difference in financial architecture can become enormous over decades.

How Dual-Channel Communication for FPV Works

What is the Promin-13 and how does it work?

Promin-13 is an autonomous aerial relay system designed to significantly extend the flight range and signal stability of FPV drones. It allows operators to work from safe shelters and bypass terrain obstacles (forests, hills, buildings) by transmitting the signal from above.

How does two-channel communication work in practice?
The video clearly demonstrates the operation of two independent data transmission channels.

ð¡ Channel 1: Remote Control > Relay Drone
Operates in the 900 MHz band (the video shows jumps across 905, 914, 925 MHz). This frequency provides maximum signal penetration and a reliable connection between the operator and the carrier drone over long distances.

ð¡ Channel 2: Relay Drone > FPV Drone
Operates in the 2.4 GHz band (we can see values like 2410, 2437, 2471 MHz). This channel is responsible for transmitting control commands directly to the strike drone from the air node.

Together, these technologies create a highly protected communication node for FPV operations at tactical distances.

One staged photograph captured a network that would reshape Silicon Valley for decades.

Fortune assembled former PayPal executives and employees in San Francisco in 2007, dressing them in suits, tracksuits, and gold chains for a mafia-themed shoot. The image included Peter Thiel, Reid Hoffman, Max Levchin, David Sacks, Roelof Botha, Jeremy Stoppelman, and Jawed Karim. Elon Musk was notably absent because he was attending an awards event. By then, PayPal had been sold to eBay for $1.5 billion, and its alumni were already building or backing companies including YouTube, LinkedIn, Yelp, Facebook, Tesla, and SpaceX.

The photo became iconic because it documented one of technologyâs most influential networks before its full impact was visible.

I posted this a couple of years ago, but thought Iâd add some additional information. 

Madsen M50 build info:

* Parts kit missing center section, but mag well intact. 

* 16 gauge sheet metal purchased from Loweâs. Slightly thinner than the kit, but it works. 

* Harbor Freight 30 inch Bending Brake to fold sheet metal repair section. 

* Cut metal strips and Tig welded to repair sections to provide the original rib look and give strength. 

* Cut and bent metal strip and Tig welded it to make trigger guard. 

* Aluminum jig made to keep it straight for welding and is a heat sink too.

label_values.value: Sigappu Rojakkal (1978) and American Psycho (2000) make for a fascinating comparison because both centre around a seemingly sophisticated, respectable man hiding a deeply disturbing and violent personality. Bharathirajaâs Sigappu Rojakkal, starring Kamal Haasan and Sridevi, was released on 28 October 1978, a remarkable 22 years before Christian Baleâs American Psycho, released in 2000. Kamal Haasanâs Dileep and Baleâs Patrick Bateman share striking similarities in their polished appearances, obsession with women, carefully maintained public personas and horrifying private lives, although the two films have very different themes and storytelling approaches. Sigappu Rojakkal is a psychological crime thriller exploring trauma, misogyny and the making of a serial killer, while American Psycho, based on Bret Easton Ellisâs 1991 novel, uses Patrick Batemanâs violent double life to satirise Wall Street culture, consumerism, status and materialism. The resemblance is fascinating, but there is no solid evidence that American Psycho was directly inspired by Sigappu Rojakkal. What makes the comparison remarkable is that Indian cinema had already explored the concept of a charming, successful-looking man concealing a murderous identity 22 years before Christian Bale's Patrick Bateman became an iconic Hollywood character. #SigappuRojakkal #AmericanPsycho #KamalHaasan #ChristianBale #IndianCinema Keywords: Sigappu Rojakkal, American Psycho, Kamal Haasan, Christian Bale, Patrick Bateman, Dileep, Bharathiraja, Sridevi, Tamil cinema, Hollywood, psychological thriller, serial killer, crime thriller, 1978 film, 2000 film, Bret Easton Ellis, Wall Street, consumerism, psychopathy, double life, cinema comparison, Indian cinema history, cult cinema, classic movies, film analysis, movie edit, cinema reels.

No degree. No traditional roadmap. Yet Peter Beck built one of the most remarkable aerospace companies in modern history by learning directly from books, experiments, and relentless curiosity. His journey proves that determination and practical knowledge can create opportunities that many people believe are impossible to reach.

Growing up in New Zealand, he developed an obsession with engineering and spent years teaching himself the principles others studied in classrooms. Instead of waiting for permission or ideal circumstances, he learned through building, testing, refining, and improving every single day.

That mindset eventually led to the launch of Rocket Lab and placed New Zealand on the global space industry map. His story demonstrates that innovation often belongs to those willing to take action while others remain focused on credentials alone.

Success rarely follows one universal formula. Sometimes the people who change industries are the ones who choose experience over convention and persistence over recognition. The willingness to keep learning and creating can become the most valuable qualification of all.

595 BTC ($38.3M) drained from 500 Bitcoin wallets in under 25 minutes on July 30.

Nobody hacked a device or tricked a user. If analysts are right, the wallets' seed phrases were never truly random to begin with, generated using a flawed process that narrowed down the possibilities enough for someone to recompute the private keys directly.

Not a single multisig wallet was touched, only single-signature ones. That detail is why analysts believe this is a seed generation flaw, not a phishing attack or stolen device.

Windows keeps a hidden second ledger called Amcache that records every executable ever run on your system, even after you delete Prefetch and remove the USB drive. This forensic artifact stores file paths, sizes, and SHA-1 hashes, surviving long after the original files are gone. Most people think clearing Prefetch erases all evidence, but Amcache operates independently and never gets the memo to delete.

Picture a guy standing next to a giant radar machine at work, and suddenly the chocolate in his pocket turns into a gooey mess. Thatâs not a lab accident story, thatâs literally how the microwave oven was born. Percy Spencer wasnât even supposed to be experimenting that day, he just noticed something weird and got curious enough to chase it. So he grabbed popcorn kernels and held them near the same tube, and watched them pop right there in the lab like some kind of magic trick. Then he got bolder and tried an egg, which exploded and splattered a coworker who made the mistake of leaning in for a closer look. Raytheon saw dollar signs fast and filed a patent that same year, and by 1947 the first commercial microwave, called the Radarange, hit the market. Except it was nothing like the countertop box you own now, this thing stood almost six feet tall, weighed 750 pounds, and cost about as much as an actual house. It even needed plumbing hookups because the tube inside ran so hot it required water cooling just to survive. Naturally it didnât end up in homes at first, it went to restaurants, railroads, and cruise ships that could actually afford the thing. What gets me is that Spencer never finished school past fifth grade and taught himself everything through library books and time in the Navy. No engineering degree, no fancy lab training, just curiosity and a melted candy bar. Would you have poked at that mystery melted chocolate, or just tossed your pants in the wash and moved on?

label_values.value:
Comment "Day 2" to get my full prompt vocabulary guide â the exact language that makes AI output look shot, not generated. 

What you're seeing was shot on IMAX. 

That's what I'd say if I was a liar. 

This was made entirely with AI. 

So why does it look real and natural instead of the default slop flooding your feed? Three things. Almost nobody does all three. 

First â stop using one model for everything. 

The single fastest way into slop territory is forcing one model to do a job it was never built for. 

Realism â Soul 2.0. Cinematic frames â Soul Cinema. Text-heavy images â GPT 2.0. General editing â Nano Banana 2.0. 

Right model, right job. That alone fixes half the problem. 

Second â prompt like you're on set with an infinite budget. 

Name the camera. Name the lens. Name the director whose eye you want. Name the film the shot should feel like. 

The model doesn't guess what "cinematic" means. It renders what you can actually name. 

Which is the real bottleneck â not the tool, your vocabulary. Most people are describing a scene with maybe twenty words of film language. A cinematographer has thousands. 

Third â add organic texture on top. 

Film grain. Halation. Bloom. 

AI output is too clean. No sensor noise, no lens imperfection, nothing a real camera would have introduced. That sterility is what your eye reads as fake before you can explain why. 

Put the imperfection back and it stops looking rendered. Dehancer if you want the proper film emulation, or just an overlay in Premiere if you want it in thirty seconds. 

Think of it like post on a real film. The footage is never the final look. The grade and the grain are what make it cinema. 

What changes when you run all three: 

1. Output that reads as shot, not generated 
2. A repeatable look instead of one lucky render 
3. Work that survives a second look on a big screen 

For anyone making stylized shorts, brand films, or cinematic sequences with AI â this is the difference between a clip and a frame that holds.

Everyone builds the same quant project. GitHub has 9,433 repos tagged LSTM and

These four are the opposite. Tail index estimation with the Hill estimator. A
Hawkes process fitted to the arrival of extreme moves. Monte Carlo Greeks by
autodiff in JAX. And the Black-Scholes free boundary by Crank-Nicolson.

In all four the code is the short part. The Hill estimator is thirty lines,
and the whole project is deciding where the tail starts.

About a month of evenings, and the last one is a week on its own. You could
finish all four and still not defend a single line of it.

Building is the easy half.

Tomorrowâs eclipse will be the first visible from mainland Europe since 1999. It happens because of a wild cosmic coincidence, the Moon is 400 times smaller than the Sun, yet also 400 times closer, meaning it fits almost exactly over the star in our sky.

Founded in 2017 and based in Gurugram, Zypp Electric is a fully tech-enabled EV Rental platform that gives gig and delivery workers access to electric two-wheelers and three-wheelers on rent.

Zypp was founded by a married couple, Akash Gupta (who comes from Jaipur and has worked at Snapdeal, Mobikwik, etc) and Rashi Agarwal (who comes from Almora and has worked at S&P Capital).

In 2021, Tushar Mehta (ex-Ola and Cars24) joined Zypp Electric as Business Head, and later became co-founder.

When Zypp began as a bootstrapped startup, the founders started with a dockless bicycle sharing model and moved to e-bike and e-scooter. 

Finally, by 2019-2020, they pivoted Zypp to EV-powered last-mile delivery.

âWe talked to gig workers directly and understood the main gap: their earnings were modest to begin with, and yet they had to bear EMIs, fuel expenses, and maintenance costs,â Rashi says.

With the vision of enabling gig workers and delivery riders to have affordable access to vehicles rather than ownership, the EV-as-a-Service model was launched. 

Today, Zypp Electric operates as a fully tech-enabled EV Rental platform that empowers gig and delivery workers.

Purchasing an EV generally requires an upfront investment of Rs 70,000 to Rs 1,20,000 or more â along with loan repayments and maintenance expenses.

Zypp weekly and daily models completely eliminate ownership costs and enables riders to save approximately Rs 5,000 to Rs 6,000 per month compared to operating petrol-powered two-wheelers.

Riders receive ready-to-use electric scooters and e-cargo three-wheelers along with a fully integrated EV ecosystem. They do not have to pay any upfront cost or EMI. Instead, they pay rent that includes vehicle access, maintenance, insurance, and battery swapping. 

To date, Zypp has empowered 2.5 lakh+ gig workers. It has also completed 20.5 million emission-free deliveries.

In FY25, it hit Rs 438-449 crore in annual revenue.

An X-ray is the simplest of the five. It uses a small amount of ionizing radiation to create a flat, 2D image, and bones show up very clearly because they absorb more X-rays than soft tissues. It is commonly used to look for fractures, chest problems, or joint abnormalities. 

A CT scan also uses X-rays, but instead of taking one flat picture, it takes many images from different angles and uses a computer to combine them into detailed cross-sectional slices of the body. This makes CT much better for seeing the shape and position of bones, organs, bleeding, and internal injuries. 

A 3D CT scan goes one step further: the same CT data is reconstructed by a computer into a three-dimensional model that can be rotated and viewed from different angles, making complex fractures, bones, blood vessels, and anatomy easier to understand.

An MRI works completely differently. It does not use X-rays or ionizing radiation. Instead, it uses a very strong magnetic field and radio waves to detect signals from hydrogen atoms in your body. Because soft tissues contain lots of water and hydrogen, MRI is particularly good at showing the brain, spinal cord, muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, and other soft tissues. 

MRI with contrast is essentially an MRI combined with a contrast agent, usually injected into a vein. The contrast changes the signal from certain tissues and makes things such as blood vessels, inflammation, tumors, infection, or areas with an abnormal blood supply stand out more clearly.

So, in simple terms: an X-ray gives you a quick 2D look, CT gives you detailed slices using X-rays, 3D CT turns those slices into a rotatable model, MRI gives you highly detailed soft-tissue images using magnets and radio waves, and MRI with contrast makes certain abnormalities and blood vessels easier to see.

This is Geiseltalsee in Germany, the country's largest artificial lake. It was created by flooding an abandoned lignite mine, a process that finished around 2011 and left an entire landscape sealed underwater. The trees, the ground, the old mine structures are all still down there, roughly 80 meters at the deepest point.

Captured by underwater photographer Alex Dawson, the reason it looks so unreal is pure science. The lake is young and extremely low in nutrients, so almost no algae grows to cloud the water. That gives you visibility most divers only dream about and that haunting glass-green color.

The trees are the strangest part. In cold, still, low-oxygen freshwater, the bacteria that normally rot wood barely function. So instead of decaying, the forest is being quietly preserved, standing exactly where it grew before the water swallowed it.

An entire world, paused underwater, hiding in plain sight.

A developer has created an open-source file transfer system called Decimen Optical Transfer that transfers files using nothing more than a screen and a camera. It doesn't require Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, a USB cable, or an internet connection.

The project was created by the GitHub developer - bashalarmistalt. According to the developer, it was built in just one night using Claude Code and has been released under the MIT License.

GitHub: https://github.com/bashalarmistalt/decimen-optical-transfer

The system works by splitting a file into thousands of small data blocks. Each block is encoded into a QR code, and the sender displays these QR codes in rapid succession at around 60 frames per second. The receiving device scans the QR codes using its camera and reconstructs the original file once enough data has been received.

To make the transfer reliable, the project uses Fountain Codes, an advanced error-correction technique that allows the receiver to recover the complete file even if many QR code frames are missed during the transfer.

According to the developer's tests, the system achieves transfer speeds of around 128-129 KB/s when the devices are handheld and up to 186-190 KB/s when they are kept completely still. At these speeds, a 2 MB image can be transferred in approximately 16-17 seconds.

The project runs entirely in a web browser, so no app installation or pairing process is required. As long as both devices have a screen, a camera, and a modern web browser, files can be transferred across different platforms.

Although it isn't designed to replace USB cables or high-speed wireless file sharing, it provides an alternative when conventional connectivity isn't available.

ð¤ Travis Scott â the concert that shook the ground
During the Utopia era, Travis Scott made headlines when crowds at his shows generated enough synchronized movement to register as seismic activity. At his 2023 concert at Romeâs ancient Circus Maximus, around 60,000 fans jumping in unison created vibrations comparable to a small 1.3-magnitude earthquake, with locals briefly fearing an actual quake. 

The moment became symbolic of the energy surrounding the Utopia era, especially during songs like FE!N, where crowds were known to erupt into nonstop bouncing and mosh pits. Similar reports later emerged from other tour stops, with seismic sensors picking up crowd-generated tremors. 

It wasnât a real tectonic earthquake, but it was powerful enough to be detected by monitoring equipment â a rare reminder of just how much energy tens of thousands of fans can create together.

label_values.value:
Before cars had digital screens telling you the outside temperature, Cadillac came up with a clever mechanical solution.

Some Cadillac models in the 1970s and 1980s had a small thermometer built into the driver's side mirror. At first glance, it just looked like part of the mirror housing, but if you looked closely, you could see a tiny temperature scale.

You might wonder, "Wouldn't the engine's heat make it inaccurate?" That's exactly why Cadillac placed it in the side mirror. The mirror sits far away from the hot engine and receives plenty of moving air while the car is driving. This gives it a much better reading of the actual outside temperature.

The thermometer itself didn't use electricity or batteries. It worked using a sealed strip or coil made from two different metals. As the air temperature changed, the metals expanded and contracted by different amounts, causing the needle to move across the temperature scale.

Think of it like an old-fashioned outdoor thermometer attached to your car. Instead of showing the temperature on a dashboard screen, you simply glanced at your side mirror.

It was a simple but practical feature that let drivers know if the weather was getting cold enough for frost or icy roads - years before digital displays became common in cars.

The right houseplants can do more than make your bedroom look good. Some may help create a calmer, more relaxing environment that makes winding down at night a little easier.

Plants like lavender and jasmine are known for their relaxing scents, while snake plants and aloe vera use a type of photosynthesis that allows them to take in carbon dioxide at night. Having greenery around may also simply make a room feel more peaceful and comfortable.

But houseplants arenât a magic sleep fix. Their effect on indoor air quality in a normal home is limited, and thereâs no strong evidence that simply putting a plant beside your bed will dramatically improve your sleep.

This footage captures a street photographer documenting the spring travel season in Le Marais, Paris, using a fully functional, WWII-era Kodak Matchbox camera. While surrounding tourists rely on smartphones equipped with advanced digital zoom and automated post-processing, this photographer utilizes a mechanical piece of history to capture the French capital on film, contrasting modern computational photography with raw analog engineering.
From a technological and engineering perspective, the Kodak Matchbox cameraâoriginally developed in 1944 for the Office of Strategic Servicesâis a masterpiece of minimalist mechanical design. Built to function covertly behind enemy lines, the camera features a fixed-focus 25mm lens and a single-speed rotary shutter packaged inside a tiny metal casing designed to be disguised with a standard matchbox label. Operating entirely without electricity, light meters, or microprocessors, it relies strictly on chemical physics and mechanical synchronization. When the shutter opens, light passes through the glass element to expose a 16mm film strip, a process governed entirely by the physical properties of silver halide crystals reacting to photons rather than algorithms reconstructing pixels.

Sanctuary Mountain Maungatautari is about an hour from Rotorua and it is one of the largest fenced ecosystems in the world.

Every rat, stoat and possum that kills New Zealand's native birds has been removed from inside the fence. The birds here are so loud it stops you in your tracks. You do not hear this anywhere else in New Zealand.

But the Moa Hunter tour is what got us. Our guide did not just walk us through the bush. He took us back to a time when MÄori were foraging this forest, hunting moa and living off the land.

We picked leaves and made tea right there on the track. He showed us how the last moa was hunted. I have done a lot of tours in this country and nothing has come close to this one.

If you are anywhere between Auckland and Rotorua, do not skip this.

Everyone says it. Nobody does the math. So I did it for you. ð§®

Hereâs what it actually costs to open a small beach bar in Thailand as a foreigner:

Visa + legal setup. You need a Thai partner holding 51%, a legitimate Thai majority company, and a work permit. That permit requires 2M THB ($55,600) in paid-up registered capital sitting in the company, plus 4 Thai employees on social security. Legal fees, company registration & accountant costs: 80k to 150k THB ($2,200 to $4,200).

Location. Forget buying land. You will lease. A genuinely beach-adjacent commercial spot in Koh Samui, Phuket, or Koh Lanta starts at 80k THB ($2,200) per month and goes well past 200k THB ($5,600). You sign a 3-year minimum and pay 3 months deposit upfront.

Build-out & setup. A proper bamboo and wood structure with a commercial kitchen, bar counter, storage, fridges, sound system, and outdoor seating runs 1.2M to 2M THB ($33,000 to $55,600). Add electricity, plumbing, and a generator backup: minimum 100k THB ($2,800) more. ð¨

Licenses. Liquor license, food service permit, and entertainment license for music. Govt fees are at 10k to 20k THB ($280 to $560) per year, but budget another 50k to 100k THB ($1,400 to $2,800) in lawyer fees to get through the process. Timeline: 2 to 4 months minimum.

Stock and opening inventory. Beer, spirits, mixers, fresh food ingredients: 80,000 to 150,000 THB ($2,200 to $4,200) for a solid opening month. ð»

Staff. 2 to 4 staff minimum. Minimum wage in tourist areas is 350 to 400 THB ($10 to $11) per day. Budget 60k to 100k THB ($1,700 to $2,800) per month total in salaries.

Monthly operating costs. Rent, staff, electricity, restocking, maintenance, Wi-Fi, insurance, accountant: 250k to 400k THB ($7,000 to $11,100) / month.

Real total: 3.5M to 5M THB. Thatâs $97,000 to $140,000 USD. More than what people think. ð

Break-even. At an average spend of 400 THB ($11) per customer and 60% margin on drinks, you need 60-100 covers per day just to cover costs. In low season on a quiet beach, itâs not guaranteed.

Good luck guys!!!

You want to wake up with morning wood because itâs one of the signs your body is recovering properly, your sleep is on point, and your hormones are doing their job. Sleep like your ancestors did in a dark room with no blue light, no notifications, and no late-night scrolling.

Stop throwing away the yolk. The yolk contains important nutrients and healthy fats your body uses to support hormone production.

Get outside and get morning sunlight. It helps regulate your body clock, improve sleep quality, and supports healthy testosterone levels.

Cold showers, tough workouts, and uncomfortable challenges build discipline. A stronger mind helps you stay consistent with building a stronger body.

Your body adapts to the stress you place on it. Progressive overload and challenging training help build muscle and support a strong physique.

The underrated habit most men ignore. A simple walk after eating can help manage blood sugar, improve digestion, reduce stress, and support overall health.

The AI simulates the lens itself. Depth, distortion, compression â the physical look of a real camera body.

Screenshot your first frame. Drop it into an AI tool and describe the look you want.

Does it only work for one type of look, like fisheye?
No. Same trick works for anamorphic, tilt-shift, and a long list of other lens styles.

A candlestick has four numbers on it. The standard way to measure how much a stock moved uses two of them.

This is whatâs in the other two.

Not a strategy. It doesnât predict the next candle and it says nothing about direction.

It measures how violent a day actually was, from data already sitting on your chart. Thatâs what risk models and volatility forecasts run on.

Turns out the wick is a real statistic with an exact constant, 4ln2 - 2. I derived it on paper and reproduced the 2025 Journal of Econometrics result in simulation.

The wild part isnât the formula. Itâs that traders stared at wicks for a century before anyone proved they were measuring something.

The product didnât change. 
The story did.

â¹100 chappals become â¹14,000 âartisanal footwearâ abroad.

Makhana becomes an expensive âsuperfood.â

A simple mala becomes a luxury wellness accessory.

Same product. Better packaging. Better positioning. Better story.

And suddenly, weâre willing to pay 10X for it.

Maybe thatâs the real lesson in marketing.

We donât always buy what something is.
We buy the story weâre told about what it is.

And once you understand that, you start noticing it everywhere.

In fashion. Food. Wellness. Luxury.

Even politics.

The most powerful product in the world might just be a good story.

A twelve-year-old in shiny silver parachute pants owns a 1992 dance recital stage like he already knows something the world does not, and three decades later that kid is Hollywood's Ken, a Jedi-adjacent star pilot, and Marvel's newly crowned Ghost Rider. Ryan Gosling's epic old dancing videos (1992) are the internet's favorite origin-story footage, the resurfaced clips of young Ryan performing full-throttle hip-hop routines with Ontario's Elite Dance Studio that fans describe as watching the Mona Lisa being painted in real time.

The mood is destiny rehearsing in sequins. The MC Hammer-styled outfit gleams, the moves hit with total commitment, and the confidence radiating off the boy from Cornwall, Ontario explains everything that followed: within a year he was cast on The All New Mickey Mouse Club alongside Britney Spears, Justin Timberlake, and Christina Aguilera, and the dance training eventually paid off at the highest levels, waltzing through the stars in his Oscar-nominated La La Land turn, then bringing down the Academy Awards with the I'm Just Ken spectacular. When the recital clips resurfaced and went viral, Gosling met them with trademark self-deprecation, joking about having peaked early, though the timeline argues otherwise: Project Hail Mary conquering 2026, Star Wars: Starfighter arriving in 2027, and the Comic-Con Hall H eruption this July when Kevin Feige announced him as Johnny Blaze in Shawn Levy's 2028 Ghost Rider, a role Gosling admitted he had wanted for a very long time. This is career storytelling in reverse, every superstar milestone traceable to one fearless kid refusing to dance small.

What makes it a must-see is the proof. Confidence is not built by fame; it was clearly there first, wearing silver pants in Ontario.

Save this post for your before-they-were-famous collection, and share it with the friend whose childhood recital tapes also deserve a Marvel announcement someday.

Despite becoming one of the biggest comedy stars in the world, Jim Carrey was actually rejected by Saturday Night Live twice. He first auditioned for the 1980-81 season, and legend has it that while he was auditioning, he saw someone else through the window of a building across the street who seemed to be "losing it," which influenced his high-energy, physical comedy style later on.

When he finally returned to host the show years later, his "Night at the Roxbury" sketch with Will Ferrell and Chris Kattan became so iconic that it was eventually turned into a full-length feature film. During his hosting gigs, Carrey was known for being so physically intense that he would often bruise himself or accidentally break props during rehearsals because he refused to "half-speed" any of his slapstick routines.

Jim Carrey joins the Roxbury Guys in their most iconic sketch for Season 21 of SNL (1996) Carrey improvised two of the sketch's most memorable moments: blowing dust off the CD and the hilarious "souvenir" dentures bit. In his 2019 autobiography Baby Don't Hurt Me, @chriskattanofficial recalls that it was writer Fred Wolf who suggested reviving the "Roxbury Guys" sketch, originally created by Kattan and Will Ferrell during their time at The Groundlings and first performed on the Phil Hartman/Gin Blossoms episode earlier that season (1996). Wolf also pitched the idea of adding host Jim Carrey as a third, head-bopping club-goer. Kattan swapped their original track, "More and More" by Captain Hollywood Project, for Haddaway's "What Is Love," giving the sketch its now-iconic soundtrack.

Working with writer Steve Koren, Kattan and Ferrell expanded the format to include multiple locations connected by pre-taped scenes of the trio driving from club to club. These were shot on Friday at 2 PM in Studio 6H, two floors down, on the Late Night with Conan O'Brien set.

The biggest thing that helped me was moving away from just straight up applying.

Instead, I started doing coffee chats and gaining referrals (but not in the way people explain it).

Hereâs what a referral actually does: it gets a human to open your application. Thatâs real and worth having.

Hereâs the best and easiest way to achieve this without overwhelming yourself.

1. Message people 1 to 2 years ahead of you, not directors or hiring managers.

They reply far more often, they remember doing this recently, and theyâre usually the ones who know whether a team is actually hiring. Theyâre also much easier to talk to since theyâre similar in age to you.

2. Then, ask for the hiring managerâs name, not the referral.

A referral goes into the same system your application does. A name means you can follow up with a specific person when it goes quiet, instead of chasing a portal. It also shows more interest than simply asking for a referral from someone, and that you actually want to expand your network in the company.

3. Volume is still king.

Most coffee chats and referrals will go nowhere no matter how well you do the first four. This only works on volume.

BONUS: Hereâs a shortcut you can use to check whether a company actually hires or just collects applications.

Can buying SSDs today make you money tomorrow? ð¾ð

Solid State Drives (SSDs) have become one of the fastest-growing components in the electronics industry, powered by demand from AI, cloud computing, gaming, and data centers. But some people are now asking a different question: Can SSDs themselves be an investment?

Unlike gold or stocks, SSDs are technology products. Their prices are influenced by the cost of NAND flash memory, supply shortages, and demand cycles. During periods of chip shortages, SSD prices can rise sharply. But over the long run, technology usually becomes cheaper as manufacturing improves.

That means buying SSDs purely as an investment is highly speculative. While prices may spike temporarily, thereâs also the risk of newer, faster storage technologies making existing models less valuable.

For most investors, companies that manufacture memory chips or storage devices may offer a more practical way to benefit from the industryâs growth than stockpiling SSDs themselves.

 Markets & Stock Pitch
	â¢ Pitch me a stock â is it undervalued or overvalued, and why?

Ratios & Valuation Basics
	â¢ What's the difference between EV and Market Cap?
	â¢ Why do we use EV/EBITDA instead of P/E in some cases?
	â¢ When would P/E give you a misleading picture?

DCF Model
	â¢ Walk me through a DCF model, start to finish.

 More common technicals

	â¢ What's the difference between Enterprise Value and Equity Value?

 How I prepped

ð Your first equity research report â the honest playbook

Most beginners try to predict the stock price.
Thatâs not research. Research = an argument backed by evidence.

Hereâs how to actually build one ð

ð¹ Start boring
Pick a company you can explain in one line â paint, biscuits, cement. Simple business + public financials = perfect first pick.

ð¹ Learn how it makes money
Where revenue comes from, who it competes with, why customers stay, and whoâs running the show.

ð¹ Read what nobody reads
The annual report â especially the MD&A, risk factors, and notes to accounts. Companies bury the truth in the fine print.

ð¹ Interrogate 5 years of numbers
Revenue trend, margins, cash flow, debt, ROE/ROCE. One year tells you nothing. The direction tells you everything.
ð¹ Value it â assumptions first
DCF, comps, multiples. The math is easy. Defending your assumptions is the real skill.

ð¹ Commit to a call
Buy / Hold / Sell. Target price. Catalysts. Risks. No verdict = no report.

Save this for when you write yours ð

My CV got me shortlisted at BCG, JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley, PwC, KPMG, EY, ZS Associates and more 

Here are a few tips that actually worked:

â Always highlight the impact you created in every role â numbers speak louder than responsibilities
â Keep it to 1 page. No exceptions.
â Font size between 10â12pt - readable but clean
â Structure it into these sections:

â Educational Qualifications & Academic Achievements
â Work Experience
â Positions of Responsibility
â Extra-Curriculars

ð A holistic CV wins -  recruiters love seeing case competitions, social impact projects, debate competitions, sports, and cultural activities alongside academics. Show them the full picture of who you are.
Your CV is your first impression - make it count 

ð Tailor your CV for every application. Don't send the same CV everywhere. Tweak your summary, highlight relevant experiences, and mirror the language used in the job description. Recruiters can tell when you've made the effort.

ð Use strong action verbs and quantify everything. Don't write "was responsible for managing a team" - write "led a team of 8 to deliver X, resulting in Y% improvement." Numbers, percentages, and outcomes make your CV stand out instantly.

ð Make sure your CV is well formatted. A cluttered CV is as bad as an empty one. Keep margins clean, use consistent spacing, and make it easy for a recruiter to skim in 30 seconds â because that's exactly how long they spend on it in the first round.

Four dead office PCs. A bedroom floor. Zero cloud APIs.

This is what it actually looks like: no rack, no server room, no rows of blinking lights. Just a mechanical keyboard on a stone floor next to a motorcycle helmet â and a cluster of used hardware quietly running an entire AI business.

The Hardware

A Dell micro desktop â the kind offices dump by the pallet during a refresh. $60. Two retired laptops, dead batteries, working CPUs. $120 each. One old tower with a cheap GPU. $120.

Total cost: $420. Every piece was somebody else's e-waste six months ago.

How It Works

They run as one machine. Small models, split by job: a 3B model handles classification on the mini PC. A 7B model handles drafting on the tower with the GPU. The laptops just watch files and manage the queue.

Nothing touches a cloud API. Nothing.

The Math That Flips Everything

Inbox triage and drafted replies: $500/month per client.
Invoice and receipt processing: $300.
Content drafting from client notes: $800.

Four clients on the middle tier â $3,200 a month. Against a $12 electricity bill.

The Punchline

Nobody in that room owns a GPU worth more than $150. The subscription stack this person cancelled cost more than the entire cluster combined.

It was landfill six months ago. Now it makes payroll.

This is the quiet version of the AI gold rush â not chasing the biggest model, just running the smallest one that gets the job done, on hardware nobody else wanted. ð¥ï¸â»ï¸ð°

Hiring is exploding in August. Most people wonât notice until itâs already over.

Recruiters just got back from vacation. Budgets are about to freeze for the year. And most job seekers have no idea any of this is happening.

Hereâs what you need to know before the window closes ð

1ï¸â£ The budget clock is ticking
Most companies lock fiscal year-end approvals in September. Managers are rushing to fill headcount right now, before it gets frozen or reallocated. August is the green light. September is too late.

2ï¸â£ Ghost jobs disappear this month
Summer postings are full of roles companies list but never fill. In August, teams need people back at their desks, so real postings return. Fewer fake listings. More real interviews.

3ï¸â£ Target the rehire wave
Companies spent July limping along understaffed. Now theyâre reposting those same roles. Search for postings that look recycled from June or July. Those are rehires, not new plans, and they move fast.

4ï¸â£ Fix whatâs actually broken first
Before you touch your resume, check the boring stuff. Is your LinkedIn set to âOpen to Workâ for recruiters only, not your whole network? Does your resume file still say âResume_Final_v2_NEWâ? Small fixes. Recruiters notice.

5ï¸â£ Apply within the first 48 hours
After that, most recruiters have already shortlisted their first 10 candidates. Turn on job alerts. Donât just browse job boards once a week.

6ï¸â£ Skip the apply button
Find who posted the role. Send a short, specific message about it. Apply after that conversation. A warm application skips the algorithm entirely.

The people landing interviews in August started prepping weeks ago. September panic is everyone elseâs disadvantage, and your edge.

A recruiter is usually thinking, If this candidate had a 3-year or 5-year gap, how quickly can they get productive after joining? Because companies are hiring for a business need.

â¢ Are their skills still relevant?
â¢ Have they kept up with industry changes?
â¢ Will they need extensive training?
â¢ Are they fully ready to return now?

Thatâs why your answer matters.

A 5-year career gap with continuous learning can sometimes be easier to hire than a 1-year gap where the candidate did nothing to stay updated.

The gap itself is not the biggest concern. Your readiness is.And thatâs exactly what recruiters are trying to assess.

# Career Gap Interview Questions | Best Answers for Freshers & Experienced (2026)

**Worried about explaining your career gap in interviews?** Here are the most common career gap interview questions with professional answer tips to help you respond confidently.

## Top Career Gap Interview Questions

1. Tell me about your career gap.
2. Why did you leave your previous job?
3. What were you doing during your career gap?
4. How did you keep your skills updated?
5. What new skills did you learn?
6. Did you take any certifications or online courses?
7. Why are you returning to work now?
8. What motivates you to restart your career?
9. How will you handle work after a long break?
10. What challenges did you face during your gap?
11. How did the gap help you grow personally?
12. Did you work on any freelance or personal projects?
13. How do you manage pressure after a career break?
14. Why should we hire you despite the gap?
15. What are your career goals now?
16. How have you prepared for this role?
17. What did you learn from your previous experience?
18. How do you stay updated with industry trends?
19. Are you comfortable learning new technologies?
20. Do you have any questions for us?

## Best Tips

* Be honest about your career gap.
* Focus on what you learned during the break.
* Highlight certifications, projects, or self-learning.
* Avoid negative comments about previous employers.
* Show confidence and a positive attitude.

UPI has changed the way India pays, but a new bill introduced in the Lok Sabha on 4 August 2026 could change how these payments are regulated in the future.

The bill removes the legal restriction that prevented charges on UPI transactions. However, this does not mean that UPI payments will suddenly become paid for everyone. As of now, there are no new charges for regular users.

According to reports, any future fee may apply only to transactions above â¹2,000 made to large merchants and retail chains. The proposed fee is expected to be around 0.3% to 0.5%, which would be paid by merchants, not customers directly. For example, a â¹10,000 purchase could attract a fee of â¹30ââ¹50.

Small businesses and local shops are expected to continue offering free UPI payments, and there is currently no GST proposed on these charges.

The key takeaway: UPI is no longer legally guaranteed to remain free forever, but for most people using it for everyday purchases, nothing changes right now.

12 LinkedIn changes = more interview calls. Steal these!

1. Toggle âOpen to Workâ off then on. It resets your visibility to the algorithm. Set to âRecruiters onlyâ to hide the green banner.

2. Settings, then Data Privacy, then Job Seeking
Preferences. Turn on every toggle.

3. Enable âResume & top job applications.â It auto-shares your CV with matching recruiters.

4. Re-upload or tweak your resume weekly. This signals activity to the algorithm.

5. Add a Canva banner: name, target role, 2-3 skills, email. 90% skip this.

6. Headline formula: [Role] | [Skills] | [Value Prop]. Not
just your job title.

7. Rewrite your About. Hook, story, personal detail,
contact info. Talk like a colleague, not a resume.

8. Use Googleâs XYZ format for bullets:
âAccomplished [X], measured by [Y], by doing [Z].â

9. Add visual proof, like decks, links, or articles, to your experience entries.

10. Reorder skills by relevance. DM close connections for specific endorsements.

11. Set your profile location to your target city.
Recruiters filter by location first.

12. Turn on hourly job alerts for target roles. Be first to apply.

Save this before your next job search.

Donât make this mistake.

Most PMs donât burn out because product management is hard.

They burn out because every PM level quietly changes their job, but nobody tells them.

APM = learner
PM = feature owner
Senior PM = outcome owner
Lead PM = people + problem multiplier
Group / Director PM = portfolio operator
CPO / Founder = company-level bet maker

The problem starts when a PM keeps behaving like the previous level.

An APM who tries to âown strategyâ before learning execution creates noise.
A PM who only writes PRDs never learns business impact.
A Senior PM who still lives in every feature detail becomes the bottleneck.
A Lead PM who canât coach other PMs becomes a reviewer, not a leader.
A Director PM who still wants to make every product decision slows the entire org down.

Thatâs why âPM is CEO of the productâ is one of the most misleading career ideas.

PMs donât become valuable by having more opinions.

They become valuable by increasing the quality of decisions around them.

The real skill is not writing perfect PRDs.
The real skill is knowing what kind of PM the company needs you to become next.

Most product content glorifies frameworks, roadmaps and stakeholder management.

Very few talk about role evolution.

And honestly, thatâs where many PMs break.

Not in the roadmap.
In the transition.

Quant math looks like one giant pile you have to swallow whole. It isnât. Itâs a sequence, and the sequence is most of the difficulty.

This is the order Iâd follow if I started from zero today. Nine topics, from high school algebra up to calibrating a volatility surface. Foundations, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistical inference, computational methods, optimization, stochastic processes, pricing.

Three things in here that other roadmaps get wrong. Optimization needs nothing past linear algebra and belongs early, not in year three. Measure theory is the second pass through stochastic calculus, not the prerequisite for it. And Bayesian methods arenât optional, because you never have the sample size the frequentist story assumes.

The catch: reading all nine takes close to two years, and at the end of it you still have nothing to show anyone. Nobody gets hired for having read Shreve. Knowing the order is half of it. Applying it is the other half, and thatâs the half that decides it.

Nature knows no borders ð

As a species weâve done a lot of carving up land and saying whose is whose. Thereâs so much  disagreement and conflict over these patches of land. We all know this. We see it on the news on a daily basis.

But beneath it all. Behind all the tension, and disputes. Lies the ground on which we as a species make our claim. The forests, valleys, mountains, glaciers, deserts, plateaus, basins, coastline, oceans, riversâ¦ I could go on and on.

These natural parts of our world know no borders. They just exist. There for us to marvel at and admire. 

Itâs refreshing to look at a map, remove all the place names and borders and just appreciate how crazy the natural world is. Remove everything else and you just see hills that stretch for miles with no barbed wire. And deserts that go on acre after acre with no person let alone border checkpoint.

This post was inspired by some of the things I have read in comment sections of recent posts. Iâm not naive, I do understand that territory is a lot more nuanced and complicated than just âletâs just all live together like a happy familyââ¦ thatâs not the purpose of this post.

The purpose of this post is to just appreciate the world without the human made constraints and restrictions. 

The natural environment doesnât recognise them, and it can be a beautiful thing to appreciate a world without them.

We all live on the same planet so collectively, Earth is all our home ð

For the purpose of this post I have decided to leave out locations. But if you really want them just let me know ð

Tom Holland's Spider-Man brought a younger, more energetic version of Peter Parker to the big screen. First appearing in Captain America: Civil War before starring in his own trilogy, Tom's portrayal focused heavily on Peter as a teenager trying to balance school, friendships, and superhero responsibilities. Unlike earlier versions, this Spider-Man felt like a genuine high-school studentâawkward, excited, sometimes reckless, but always trying to do the right thing. His enthusiasm, humor, and emotional vulnerability helped make the character relatable to a new generation of fans.

What makes Tom Holland's Spider-Man so popular is the balance between comedy and responsibility. Peter often makes mistakes, gets overwhelmed, and struggles with the consequences of his actions, which gives the character room to grow throughout the films. His relationships with mentors, friends, and family members add emotional depth while the action scenes showcase Spider-Man's agility, intelligence, and courage. The combination of youthful energy, humor, heart, and heroic determination is exactly why Tom Holland's Spider-Man became one of the most beloved versions of the character in modern cinema.

Some countries are widely known for having large commercial sex industries due to tourism, legal frameworks, and historical or economic factors. The Netherlands is famous for Amsterdam's regulated Red Light District, where sex work is legal under strict regulations. Germany has one of the world's largest legal and regulated sex work industries, with licensed establishments. Thailand is internationally associated with sex tourism, although prostitution is officially illegal and enforcement varies. Brazil is known for its vibrant nightlife, and while prostitution itself is legal, many related activities are regulated or prohibited. The Philippines has long been linked to entertainment districts and sex tourism, despite prostitution being illegal. These situations are shaped by complex social, economic, legal, and cultural factors. It is important to distinguish between voluntary adult sex work and human trafficking, which is a serious crime and a violation of human rights. Laws and enforcement differ significantly across countries, and governments continue to address exploitation and trafficking through legal reforms and international cooperation.

label_values.value: Tommy Shelbyâs wedding to Grace in Peaky Blinders Season 3, one of the most memorable things about the episode is that there is no major fight scene during the wedding itself. Instead of the usual violence that the series is famous for, the wedding is filled with tension, emotion, and hidden conflict. Tommy desperately wants the day to be peaceful because it is one of the rare moments where he tries to separate his family life from the criminal world. The Shelby family, the Irish guests, and Graceâs wealthy relatives all come together under one roof, creating an atmosphere full of uneasiness and class differences. Tommy repeatedly warns his brothers and the rest of the Peaky Blinders to behave themselves and avoid causing trouble. Rather than physical fighting, the drama comes from suspicious conversations, old war memories, political secrets, and Tommyâs growing anxiety about the dangerous business deal he is about to enter. The wedding appears beautifu on the surface, with music, celebration, and family gathering, but underneath it all there is a sense that danger is waiting around the corner. This makes the episode unique because the conflict is psychological rather than physical. The absence of a big fight scene allows viewers to focus on Tommyâs happiness with Grace and the fragile peace he is trying to create before his criminal life once again drags him into violence and tragedy. Great businesses often begin with solving a simple problem rather than chasing massive profits. George Clooney and his partners set out to create a smoother tequila they genuinely enjoyed. By refining the product over time and sharing it with friends, they built strong demand before expanding commercially. Their journey demonstrates how patience, consistent quality, and understanding customer preferences can turn a small idea into an extraordinary business opportunity.

The success of Casamigos highlights an important entrepreneurial lesson. Brands that deliver real value and build trust with customers often create lasting success beyond the reputation of their founders. Strong products and clear vision remain the foundation of sustainable growth.

Every successful venture starts with identifying a need and committing to excellence. Innovation, persistence, and a dedication to creating something people truly appreciate can transform a simple idea into a legacy that continues to grow for years to come.

On June 28, 1914, in the streets of Sarajevo, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were assassinated by Gavrilo Princip. What seemed like a localized political crime immediately set off a catastrophic domino effect across the European continent. Bound by a complex web of military alliances, secret treaties, and rising imperial tensions, major global powers were pulled into a conflict of unprecedented scale. Within weeks, the assassination triggered the outbreak of World War I, a devastating total war that reshaped geopolitical borders, collapsed empires, and cost tens of millions of lives. In The Kingâs Man (2021), director Matthew Vaughn tackles this monumental historical turning point, depicting the high-stakes political intrigue and the fragile state of Europe leading up to the fatal gunfire. Through breathtaking cinematography, intense choreography, and historical atmosphere, the film illustrates how a single event in Sarajevo became the catalyst for global devastation. âWould you trust an SC/ST doctor?â

Itâs a question that gets asked far too often. But the real question is: why is caste being treated as a measure of competence?

Every doctor in India, regardless of caste, has to complete the same MBBS curriculum, pass the same university examinations, undergo the same internship, and meet the same licensing requirements to practice medicine.

Reservation is an admission policy, not a medical degree. It does not exempt anyone from passing exams or becoming a competent doctor.

Ironically, many people who question SC/ST doctors have no problem with management quota admissions or other forms of privilege. The skepticism appears only when the beneficiary belongs to a historically marginalized community.

A doctorâs ability is determined by their knowledge, training, ethics, and experience, not by their caste.

If someoneâs first instinct is to ask whether an SC/ST doctor can be trusted, the problem isnât the doctor. Itâs the caste prejudice behind the question.

Letâs stop judging doctors by their caste and start judging them by the quality of care they provide.
